children.text: tad evaṃ prathamadvitīyatṛtīyapādaiḥ samādhitatsādhanatadvibhūtayaḥ prādhānyena vyutpāditāḥ ||
children.translated_text: Thus, in the first, second, and third pādas, <s>samādhi</s> (meditative absorption), its means, and its powers have chiefly been explained.
The remaining material was stated incidentally or by way of introduction.
Now, here, <s>kaivalya</s> (isolation), which results from that, must be explained.

children.text: na caitatkaivalyabhāgīyaṃ cittaṃ paralokaṃ ca paralokinaṃ vijñānātiriktaṃ cittakaraṇasukhādyātmakaśabdādyupabhoktāram ātmānaṃ ca prasaṃkhyānaparamakāṣṭhāṃ ca vinā vyutpādya śakyaṃ vaktumiti tad etat sarvam atra pāde vyutpādanīyam itaracca prasaṅgād upodghātād vā ||
children.translated_text: And this cannot be explained without setting forth the mind that conduces to <s>kaivalya</s>, the other world and the one who passes to it, the Self—distinct from cognition and, using the mind as its instrument, the experiencer of sound and the other objects whose nature is pleasure and the like—and the highest culmination of discriminative knowledge. Therefore all this must be explained in this pāda, and other matters too, incidentally or by way of introduction.

children.text: tatra prathamaṃ siddhacitteṣu kaivalyabhāgīyaṃ cittaṃ nirdhārayitukāmaḥ pañcatayīṃ siddhim āha janmauṣadhimantratapaḥsamādhijāḥ siddhayaḥ ||
children.translated_text: First, wishing to ascertain which mind among perfected minds conduces to <s>kaivalya</s>, he states the fivefold sources of perfection: “Powers arise from birth, herbs, mantra, austerity, and <s>samādhi</s>.”
He explains [those arising from birth] with the words “in another body.”

children.text: svargopabhogabhāgīyāt karmaṇo manuṣyajātīyācaritāt kutaścin nimittāl labdhaparipākāt kvacid devanikāye jātamātrasyaiva divyadehāntaritā siddhiraṇimādyā bhavatīti ||
children.translated_text: When some karma, performed in a human birth and destined to yield enjoyment in heaven, reaches maturity through some occasion, a person is born in a particular class of gods; from the very moment of birth, powers such as minuteness arise, embodied in that divine body.
He describes perfection produced by herbs with the words “in the dwellings of the <s>Asuras</s>.”

children.text: manuṣyo hi kutaścinnimittād asurabhavanam upasaṃprāptaḥ kamanīyābhir asurakanyābhir upanītaṃ rasāyanam upayujyājarāmaraṇatvam anyāśca siddhīr āsādayati ||
children.translated_text: For a human who, through some circumstance, has reached an <s>Asura</s> dwelling obtains freedom from aging and death, as well as other powers, by consuming an elixir brought by charming <s>Asura</s> maidens.

children.text: ihaiva vā rasāyanopayogena yathā māṇḍavyo munī rasopayogād vindhyavāsīti ||
children.translated_text: Or this may occur in this very world through the use of an elixir, as with the sage <s>Māṇḍavya</s>, or, through the use of mercury, with <s>Vindhyavāsin</s>.
He describes perfection produced by mantra with the words “by mantras.”
He describes perfection produced by austerity with the word “by austerity.”
He describes the power of resolve with the expression “assuming any desired form.”
Whatever power, such as minuteness, he desires becomes his in an instant.

children.text: yatra kāmayate śrotuṃ vā mantuṃ vā tatra tadeva śṛṇoti manute veti ||
children.translated_text: Wherever he desires to hear or to think, there he hears or thinks that very thing.
By the word “and so forth,” seeing and the other faculties are included.
The powers arising from <s>samādhi</s> were explained in the preceding pāda.
